messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Non-profit Worker
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Harm: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings, Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building, Sit With Back to Wall: always sit with back against a wall to see the room
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
  Negative Appraisals: Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Clinical Vignette: Rajesh

Rajesh was sixty-eight when he finally made the call to a trauma therapist, though the event that had upended his life had occurred nearly five years prior. He had been volunteering at a community centre in the city's south side, helping young people navigate the social services system—work that had given him purpose after his divorce a decade earlier. One evening in late spring, after everyone had left, a man had forced his way into the storage room where Rajesh was organizing supplies. What followed was brutal and swift. The attacker had come from behind, had covered his mouth, had spoken in a low, threatening voice—commands Rajesh still heard in his head at odd moments, sometimes so vivid he would jolt upright in bed. The physical pain had been severe and had lingered for weeks. Even now, certain sensations—pressure on his shoulders, the smell of sweat and cologne—could send sharp, burning sensations through his lower back and pelvis, as though the trauma were being re-enacted in his own body.

In the months after, Rajesh had tried to convince himself he would recover. He returned to work, but something had fractured. He began to notice how hypervigilant he had become—every unexpected sound, every footstep in the hallway, sent his heart racing. At the community centre, he found himself unable to focus on the young people he was meant to serve; instead, he was listening, always listening, for the creak of a door, the approach of footsteps. He had come to believe that his inability to simply move past the assault revealed him as a fundamentally weak person, incapable of managing adversity the way others did. This conviction—that he was a lousy coper, that his very reactions proved his inadequacy—seemed to make everything worse. The more he judged himself for his startle responses, for his need to position himself with his back against the wall in any room, the more these behaviours intensified. What frightened him most was the thought that he would never feel anything like normal again, that some essential part of him had been permanently severed. These dark certainties fed his threat vigilance; every sound became a potential danger, every unexpected touch a violation waiting to happen.

Within a year, Rajesh had stopped going to the office. He told his supervisor he was taking medical leave, but the truth was more complicated. Being alone in the building—even during daylight—had become unbearable. The memories would surface without warning: the pressure of hands, the voice, the helplessness. When they came, they brought not just emotional distress but physical agony, and the sounds from that night would echo in his mind so clearly he could not distinguish them from present reality. The pain and the auditory flashbacks together were overwhelming, and Rajesh discovered that if he hurt himself—pressing his fingernails into his palm, holding ice until his skin burned—the physical sensation could momentarily override the memory. It was a crude solution, but it worked. Over time, he found himself relying on it more and more, and each time he did, he felt a fresh wave of shame. Here was proof, he thought, that he was falling apart, that he was not the kind of man who could endure hardship. This self-condemnation only sharpened his sense of being an outsider, fundamentally different from everyone around him, permanently marked by what had happened.

The cycle had tightened steadily. His avoidance of solitude meant he began accepting dinner invitations he did not want, sitting rigidly at tables with friends who noticed his stiffness and stopped inviting him. His need to sit with his back to the wall made him appear paranoid; people found it unsettling. When someone reached out to touch his shoulder in greeting, he would flinch violently, and the awkwardness that followed only deepened his conviction that he was now an outsider in his own social world. The intrusive memories—the sounds, the pain—kept him trapped in a state of constant threat, and the maladaptive strategies he used to manage them only reinforced his belief that he was broken beyond repair. His threat monitoring had become so acute that he had installed additional locks on his apartment door and had begun sleeping with a baseball bat within arm's reach, behaviours that seemed reasonable to him in the moment but that he recognized, on some level, were the actions of a man whose mind had turned against him. He had not returned to the community centre in four years. His last meaningful conversation with a colleague had been eighteen months ago.

What finally brought Rajesh to seek help was a moment of quiet recognition: he was sitting alone in his apartment one evening, his back against the wall, listening to the ambient sounds of the building, when he realized he could not remember the last time he had felt anything other than fear or shame. The thought terrified him more than any sound ever could. He was not certain that therapy could undo what had been done to him, but he had begun to suspect that staying as he was—trapped in this loop of hypervigilance, self-harm, and self-condemnation—was itself a kind of violence. He wanted to know if it was possible to feel human again, or whether, as he feared, that version of himself was truly gone forever.
